corrected_value.title: Clinical applications of procedures to promote the emergence of untrained intraverbal relations with children with autism.

decisions.quote: Shillingsburg, Frampton, Cleveland, and Cariveau (2018) taught listener and tact by feature, name-feature intraverbal, and feature-name intraverbal responses across sets and reported emergence of responses that were not directly trained for 6 individuals diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The current study was a systematic replication with the addition of instructive feedback (IF) with 2 children diagnosed with ASD. During trials for previously mastered listener by name responses (e.g., "Point to Tennessee" and child selects a picture of Tennessee), the experimenters provided related IF (e.g., "The capital of this state is Nashville"). After 3 sessions, we evaluated the effects of IF on related verbal responses (e.g., listener by feature, tact by feature, name-feature intraverbal, and feature-name intraverbal) across sets probes. We observed increased correct responses for related verbal responses; replicating Shillingsburg et al.
decisions.reason: The source abstract (Frampton & Shillingsburg, 2020, DOI 10.1002/jaba.659) explicitly states that Shillingsburg, Frampton, Cleveland, and Cariveau (2018) taught listener and tact by feature, name-feature intraverbal, and feature-name intraverbal responses across sets and reported the emergence of untrained responses in 6 individuals with ASD, and that the current study was a systematic replication with the addition of instructive feedback with 2 children with ASD, observing increased correct responses for related verbal responses replicating Shillingsburg et al. The supplied publisher reference entry on line 9 of 4778452caf8b412e.txt (and bibliography_metadata.json) confirms the exact original identity: Shillingsburg, M. A., Frampton, S. E., Cleveland, S. A., & Cariveau, T. (2018), Learning and Motivation, 62, 51-66, DOI 10.1016/j.lmot.2017.02.003. The sole shipped row (row 423, Tullis, Gibbs, Priester, & Tillem, 2021, Behavioral Interventions, DOI 10.1002/bin.1836) is a later 2021 article by different authors in a different journal, not an alternate report of the 2018 original. Prior adjudication and state files were checked and do not exist (never previously adjudicated).

decisions.quote: Though low-cost value affirmation interventions have been shown to reduce achievement gaps in some classroom settings, these findings have not been consistently replicated. In this study, we test the efficacy of this intervention among a new sample of students enrolled in a community college in the Midwest.

While the abstract states that low-cost value affirmation interventions have been shown to reduce achievement gaps in some classroom settings and tests the efficacy of this intervention in a new community college sample, it does not name any specific original study. decisions.location: Abstract (lines 32-37); see also Section 2, The Experiment (lines 120-130), Section 4.1 Results (lines 308-343), and Section 5.2 Discussion (lines 760-772) of 0ab1768ae9c6e310.txt
decisions.quote:
We report a replication experiment of a mechanized version of the seminal wide-screen/narrow-screen design of Wilcox and
           Baillargeon (1998) with 9.5-month-old infants (𝑁 = 80). Two different methodologies were employed simultaneously: (a) the
           standard looking time paradigm and (b) eye tracking. Across conditions with three different screen sizes, the results from both
           methodologies revealed a clear and interesting pattern: the looking times increased as a significantly linear function of reduced
           screen sizes, that is, independently of the number of different objects involved. There was no indication in the data that the infants
           made use of the featural differences between the different-looking objects involved.
decisions.reason: Full-text inspection of 0ab1768ae9c6e310.txt (Krøjgaard, Kingo, & Staugaard, 2013, DOI 10.1155/2013/639702) establishes that the sole empirical replication target of this experiment is Wilcox & Baillargeon (1998, Cognitive Psychology, 37(2), 97-155, DOI 10.1006/cogp.1998.0690, Reference [4, Exp. 3]), which is already present as shipped row 168 (target_index 0). In the Abstract (lines 32-37), Section 2 (lines 120-130), Section 4.1 Results (lines 308-343), and Section 5 Discussion (lines 690-694), the authors explicitly state that their experiment with 9.5-month-old infants was designed to replicate Reference [4, Exp. 3] ('the reference study') and that Condition 2 (Narrow-Control, counterbalancing ball-ball and box-box trials) was added as a control condition to test the featural discrimination assumption of [4, Exp. 3] (explicitly citing 'cf. [4, page 118]' when reporting the planned Narrow-Test vs. Narrow-Control ANOVA in Results, lines 315-343). Candidate target_index 1 (Reference [5], Wilcox & Baillargeon, 1998, Developmental Science, 1(1), 127-142, which tested 7.5- and 4.5-month-old infants using a ball-ball control) is cited in Method (line 233) only as one of the 'Later replications [5, 20] of the original design' and is never cited in Section 2 (The Experiment) or Section 4 (Results). Although the blind coding treated Reference [5] as a second retested target based on Section 5.2 (lines 760-772), Section 5.2 merely discusses the authors' Moving Object as Attractor (MOA) hypothesis in relation to prior literature ('For example, in their followup to the reference study, Wilcox and Baillargeon [5] obtained... see also [23]') and explains why [5] differed in infant age (4.5 and 7.5 months vs. 9.5 months) and stimulus counterbalancing. Under the codebook, an earlier follow-up/replication study discussed as literature comparison while the experiment itself replicates [4, Exp. 3] with an added control condition is not a separate retested target.

decisions.location: Introduction, The proposed research (lines 183-195; see also lines 260-264) of 0e4a00331066c9e6.txt
decisions.quote:
The goal of the current research was twofold. First, we intended to replicate Carney
et al.’s (2010) main eﬀects and to test the possibility that the relationship between
embodied power and risk-taking is statistically mediated by increases in testosterone. As
described below, we used Carney et al.’s (2010) reported eﬀect sizes as a guide for
estimating a suﬃciently powered sample size. Further, we followed Carney et al.’s (2010)
procedures more closely than Ranehill et al. (2015) in their replication attempt. Our
second goal was to test the possibility that elevated levels of testosterone increase
overconﬁdence, which in turn may facilitate risk-taking (see Figure 1).
   We positioned overconﬁdence within our proposed model as there is empirical work
linking people’s sense of inﬂated conﬁdence to two of Carney et al.’s (2010) three critical
variables – power (Fast, Sivanathan, Mayer, & Galinsky, 2012) and risk-taking (Camerer &
Lovallo, 1999; Campbell, Goodie, & Foster, 2004; Malmendier & Tate, 2008) – and a
theoretical rationale for why we might expect a relationship with testosterone.
decisions.reason: Full-text inspection of 0e4a00331066c9e6.txt (Ronay, Tybur, van Huijstee, & Morssinkhof, 2017, DOI 10.1080/23743603.2016.1248081) confirms that the paper's empirical replication target is Carney, Cuddy, & Yap (2010, DOI 10.1177/0956797610383437), which is already represented by shipped row 1047 (target_index 0). Candidate target_index 1 (Fast, Sivanathan, Mayer, & Galinsky, 2012, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 117, 249-260, DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2011.11.009) manipulated power via episodic recall, role assignment, and extant work-related power, not postural power posing. In the Abstract (lines 74-84) and Introduction (lines 183-195, 213-219, 260-264), Ronay et al. explicitly state that Fast et al. (2012) was cited as background motivation for adding an overconfidence measure as a novel theoretical extension ('our extended hypotheses') to test whether testosterone and overconfidence mediate the relationship between power posing and risk-taking in their attempted replication of Carney et al. (2010). Fast et al. (2012) is never cited in the Method, Results, or Discussion. Per the codebook and review instructions, background motivation for an extension added to a replication of Study X does not constitute a separate retested target. Prior adjudication and state files were checked and do not exist.

decisions.location: Introduction (lines 138-151; see also Discussion lines 491-494) of 0e4a00331066c9e6.txt
decisions.quote:
Alternatively, the relationship
between embodied power and risk-taking may be jointly mediated by the interaction
between testosterone and cortisol. Mehta and Josephs (2010) have proposed a “dual
hormone hypothesis,” whereby cortisol modulates the eﬀect of testosterone on beha-
vior, such as risk-taking (Mehta, Welker, Zilioli, & Carré, 2015). Because Carney et al.
(2010) found high-power poses to both increase testosterone and decrease cortisol, the
interaction between these eﬀects may predict risk-taking, as has been previously shown
(Mehta et al., 2015). Furthermore, although Ranehill et al. (2015) failed to replicate
Carney et al.’s (2010) eﬀects of power posing on hormonal changes, other manipulations
related to power, such as winning a competition, have been shown to jointly impact
testosterone and cortisol (e.g. see Hamilton, Carré, Mehta, Olmstead, & Whitaker, 2015).
Thus, in the present research, we measured both testosterone and cortisol at two time
points, as per Carney et al.’s (2010) original design and tested for both main and
interactive eﬀects.
decisions.reason: Full-text inspection of 0e4a00331066c9e6.txt (Ronay, Tybur, van Huijstee, & Morssinkhof, 2017, DOI 10.1080/23743603.2016.1248081) confirms that candidate target_index 2 (Mehta, Welker, Zilioli, & Carré, 2015, Psychoneuroendocrinology, 56, 88-99, DOI 10.1016/j.psyneuen.2015.02.023) is cited only in a single paragraph of the Introduction (lines 138-151) alongside Mehta & Josephs (2010) and Hamilton et al. (2015) to motivate an exploratory extension testing whether the interaction between testosterone and cortisol mediates the relationship between power posing and risk-taking using the hormone measurements collected 'as per Carney et al.’s (2010) original design'. Mehta et al. (2015) is never mentioned in the Abstract, 'The proposed research' section (lines 183-204), Method, Results, or Discussion; in the Discussion (lines 491-494), the authors explicitly refer to the testosterone-by-cortisol test as 'the additionally proposed interaction between testosterone and cortisol' in contrast to their replication of Carney et al. (2010) (shipped row 1047). Under the codebook, citing a dual-hormone paper to motivate an extended interaction test within a replication of Carney et al. (2010) does not make Mehta et al. (2015) an empirically retested replication target. Prior adjudication and state files were checked and do not exist.
